---
title: "Using trendspull from R"
output: html_document
---

R calls the same Python collector through `reticulate`. The result is a regular
`data.frame`; no CSV transfer is required. Python 3.9+ and GitHub SSH access are
required while the repository is private.

Install once, in a fresh R session (Linux/macOS virtualenv setup):

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("reticulate")
reticulate::py_install(
  "git+ssh://git@github.com/maxwellkonnaris/trendspull.git@main",
  envname = "r-trendspull", method = "virtualenv", pip = TRUE
)
```

Then select that environment and collect data:

```{r collect, eval=FALSE}
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("r-trendspull", required = TRUE)
trends <- import("trendspull")

data <- trends$pull_trends(
  c("wildfire", "smoke"),
  start = "2021-01-01", end = "2025-12-31", geo = "US-CA",
  min_gap_days = 28L
)
head(data[c("date", "keyword", "value")])
```

`28L` is an R integer: this example keeps dates at least 28 elapsed days apart,
anchored at the first timestamp Google returns. Omit `min_gap_days` to keep all
dates. All keywords at a selected date stay together and retain their shared Google
scale. The value 28 is illustrative; it is not a promise of zero autocorrelation
or independence. Time-series dependence needs assessment in the later analysis.

Zeros and missing quality flags are preserved. Dates are POSIXct timestamps with
the same instants as Python's UTC timestamps. R can display them in local time;
use `format(data$date, tz = "UTC")` when checking the UTC labels.

To save the result:

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(data, "trends.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")
```

For full provenance, pass `archive = "data"` to save the complete raw response and
manifest, including dates omitted from the returned table. Alternatively, preserve
the Python metadata in an R attribute explicitly:

```{r metadata, eval=FALSE}
trends <- import("trendspull", convert = FALSE)
result <- trends$pull_trends(
  c("wildfire", "smoke"), "2021-01-01", "2025-12-31", geo = "US-CA"
)
data <- py_to_r(result)
attr(data, "trendspull") <- py_to_r(result$attrs$get("trendspull"))
```

If Python has already been initialized in the wrong environment, restart R before
calling `use_virtualenv()`. Integer-only options such as `category`, `max_attempts`
and `min_gap_days` need the R `L` suffix when supplied, for example `category = 0L`.
On Windows, install into a Conda environment with `py_install(method = "conda", ...,
pip = TRUE)` and select it with `use_condaenv()` instead of `use_virtualenv()`.
